chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr from Tha'laba from Zurara from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

"Every oath by which a man swears that he will not do something, from among those in which he has benefit in this world and the Hereafter, there is no expiation (kaffarah) upon him. And indeed, the expiation is for when a man swears, 'By Allah, I will not commit adultery,' or 'By Allah, I will not drink,' or 'By Allah, I will not betray,' and similar things, and 'I will not disobey,' then he does it, so upon him is the expiation."

key_terms.أَنْ لَا يَفْعَلَهَا: That he will not do it (refraining from an act)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between an oath that requires expiation and one that does not in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) clarifies that the obligation of expiation (kaffarah) applies specifically to oaths of abstention from major sins or disobedience, such as 'I will not commit adultery,' rather than general oaths to refrain from beneficial acts. This distinction highlights the juristic principle that breaking an oath to avoid a sin constitutes a violation of the oath's intent, whereas refraining from a permissible benefit does not carry the same weight of religious transgression. This ruling is foundational in Shia fiqh for determining when a believer must offer kaffarah for breaking a vow.
